# The browser data tools

<!-- Generated by electe-web/scripts/export-tools-repo.ts from electe-migration@8e52bf6 on 2026-09-29. Do not edit here: change the source and re-export. -->

3 tools take a table or a series and hand back a chart or a file. Nothing is uploaded: parsing, binning and merging run in the browser, and the pure parts are `src/data.ts`, tested in `src/data.test.ts`.

| function | what it does |
|---|---|
| `parseSeries(text)` | numbers out of a pasted blob; separators are comma, semicolon, whitespace or newline; the decimal is a point |
| `histogram(values, bins)` | equal-width bins, the last one closed at the top so the maximum is not lost; a constant series gets one bin |
| `suggestedBins(n)` | Sturges' rule, ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1 — the same default spreadsheets use |
| `sniffDelimiter(text)` | comma, semicolon or tab, from the header line |
| `parseDelimited(text, delimiter?)` | a CSV with quoted fields and embedded delimiters, into a `Table` |
| `mergeTables(tables)` | several tables into one, columns matched by header name, not position |
| `toCsv(table, delimiter?)` | back to CSV, quoting what needs quoting |
| `numericColumns(table)` | the columns a chart can plot |

### Histogram generator

`istogramma` · [English](https://tools.electe.net/histogram-generator) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/istogramma-con-excel)

See the shape of a set of numbers, not just its average.

**Formula.** Bin width = (max − min) ÷ number of bins    ·    default bins = ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1 (Sturges)

An average tells you where a set of numbers sits; a histogram tells you what it looks like. Two datasets with the same mean can be a tight cluster and a pair of distant humps, and only one of those is a business you can plan around. The bin count defaults to Sturges' rule — the same one spreadsheets use, so the shape matches what you would get in Excel — and stays editable, because bin width changes what a histogram appears to say and a tool that picks silently is hiding its most consequential setting.

### Merge CSV files

`unire-csv` · [English](https://tools.electe.net/merge-csv-files) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/unire-file-csv)

Combine several CSVs into one, matching columns by name.

**Formula.** Columns = the union of every file's headers, in first-seen order · rows keep their own file's values, matched by header name

Files are matched by COLUMN NAME, not by position. Position-matching is what a quick script does and it silently puts one file's revenue under another's cost the moment an export has an extra field — a mistake that survives all the way into a report because both columns hold plausible numbers. A column a file does not have comes through empty rather than shifting everything after it. The delimiter is detected per file, counted outside quoted fields, so a semicolon export with commas inside its address column is read correctly.

### Chart maker

`data-viz` · [English](https://tools.electe.net/chart-maker) · [Italian](https://tools.electe.net/it/data-visualization-free)

Paste a table, get a chart you can read.

**Formula.** One axis, always — every series is drawn on the same scale

Paste a table with a header row and the first non-numeric column becomes the labels; every numeric column is offered as a series. All of them share one axis, deliberately: two measures of different magnitude on two y-axes is the most common charting mistake there is, because the point where the lines cross is an artefact of where the axes were pinned and readers take it for a finding. If you need to compare a small number with a large one, index both to a common base or use two charts. Five series maximum — the colours are checked to stay distinguishable for colour-blind readers, and a sixth would need an unchecked one.
